Overall: the pain point is real and the wedge is sensible, but the core US culinary-education market is too small to support a venture-scale standalone company, and the exit path depends almost entirely on expansion beyond it.

Market size and attractiveness: The team's own math (several hundred programs x a few thousand dollars/year) yields a low single-digit million dollar TAM, and the program count is unverified. Even at an unrealistic 50% penetration, revenue would be well under $2M/year. Pricing per instructor seat (several hundred dollars, 3-10 seats per program) is consistent with that figure but untested with actual purchase decisions. Education buyers are budget-constrained and slow (department budgets, CTE funds, procurement cycles), and the team admits instructors can partly replicate the product with spreadsheets, so willingness to pay is unproven. Zero paying customers and 40 student trial users is encouraging for product feedback but is not market validation. Structural positives: the problem is genuine (graduates lack costing skills, chefs confirm it), the integration of costing plus allergens plus assignment generation is a differentiated workflow, and the cost to build and serve is low, so this can be a capital-efficient, profitable niche business.

Targeting the right group: Culinary instructors and programs are a reasonable beachhead because they are reachable, have an acute workload problem, and can validate the product quickly. But the buyer and user are split: instructors feel the pain while department heads and CTE administrators control budgets. The plan should clarify who signs and who champions. High school CTE programs are numerous and have dedicated funding streams, which could make them a more attractive segment than private schools, but also bring heavier procurement friction. The more promising targets are adjacent: hospitality management programs (much larger enrollments and a broader curriculum footprint including F&B cost control), restaurant group onboarding and training (larger budgets, faster purchasing, willingness to pay for operational outcomes), and continuing education/certification bodies (e.g., food safety and allergen training, where allergen compliance has regulatory and liability weight). These groups are mentioned only as 'later opportunities' and deserve earlier testing, since they determine whether this is a company or a feature.

Scalability: As a pure culinary-school tool, scale is capped by market size, not by execution. Expansion paths exist: hospitality programs, international culinary schools, corporate training, allergen compliance tooling, and possibly licensing the costing and allergen engine to other platforms. However, each adds product requirements (regional pricing, batch recipes, different buyer types) and the dependence on third-party pricing data is a margin and reliability risk that scales with usage. Consulting revenue (conversion and alignment) is useful for early cash and learning but is non-scalable and could dilute focus. Competitive risk is meaningful: restaurant costing vendors or LMS/education platforms could add an education mode, and the moat today is workflow and curriculum content rather than proprietary technology or data.

Exit potential: Venture-scale outcomes appear unlikely on the current scope. Realistic outcomes are (1) a profitable lifestyle or small bootstrapped business in the $500K-$3M revenue range, (2) a tuck-in acquisition by a foodservice software company, a hospitality education publisher (textbook and courseware providers are natural acquirers, since their fixed-price exercises are the stale alternative), or an LMS/edtech player seeking vertical content, with likely valuations in the low single-digit millions, or (3) a larger outcome only if the product expands into operator training and compliance with proven revenue across multiple segments. Strategic acquirers would value usage data, curriculum adoption and recipe/lesson libraries, so early traction with many programs matters more than early revenue.

Answer to the team's question: as a standalone company in the current framing, the market is likely too small; positioning as a feature or content product within a broader hospitality education or foodservice training offering is the more defensible path unless early pilots show strong pull from larger adjacent segments. Recommended next steps: verify the program count and enrollment data, run paid pilots with real price points to test willingness to pay, test one adjacent segment (hospitality management or restaurant-group training) in parallel, and recruit a foodservice or education-sales advisor. Paid pilots at three to five programs are the right use of funds because they directly resolve the biggest uncertainty (whether anyone pays), but expect this to be a niche, modestly sized business unless expansion is demonstrated.

Business plan text:

Menuschool
Menuschool: Executive Summary
The Problem
Culinary students spend much of their training learning to cook, but far less time learning to
run the numbers behind a menu. Food cost, portion yield, and pricing are what decide whether a
restaurant survives, yet many programs teach these topics with handouts, spreadsheets, or
textbook examples that use outdated or made-up prices. Instructors we spoke with told us they
want to teach costing with real data, but building costed lesson plans by hand takes a long
time. A single recipe can have fifteen or twenty ingredients, each with different purchase
units, trim loss, and yields, and prices change often.
Allergen labeling is a second gap. Students are expected to know the major allergens and how to
communicate them on a menu, but instructors usually cover this in a separate lecture instead of
building it into every recipe students work with. As a result, costing and allergen awareness
are taught as isolated topics instead of as part of one menu planning process.
The result is that graduates often enter kitchens without practical experience in menu costing.
Several chefs we interviewed said this is one of the first things they have to teach new hires.
Our Solution
Menuschool is a software platform and consulting service that converts instructors' recipes
into costed, allergen-labeled digital lesson plans. An instructor enters or uploads a recipe.
The software matches each ingredient to a pricing database, applies purchase unit conversions
and yield factors, calculates cost per portion and food-cost percentage, and flags the major
allergens. The instructor can then turn the recipe into an assignment, for example asking
students to reduce the food-cost percentage below a target without removing an allergen
warning, or to build a three-course menu within a budget.
Students see the same data the instructor sees and can change ingredients, portions, and menu
prices to watch the numbers move. The goal is for menu planning to feel like a real decision
with trade-offs, not a worksheet.
The consulting side supports programs that have large recipe collections and little time. We
convert existing recipes into the platform, set up pricing sources, and help instructors map
lesson plans to their course outcomes.
Market
Our initial customers are culinary programs in the United States, including community college
programs, private culinary schools, and some high school career and technical programs. Based
on our own count from public program listings, there are roughly several hundred such programs
nationally, though we have not yet verified this figure against an authoritative source. We
estimate each program has between three and ten instructors who teach some form of menu
planning or cost control.
If we assume an average program pays a few thousand dollars per year, the addressable market in
the United States is in the low single-digit millions of dollars annually. This is a small
market on its own, which is why we see it as a starting point. Later opportunities include
hospitality management programs, corporate training for restaurant groups, and continuing
education for working cooks.
Business Model
We plan three sources of revenue. First, annual program licenses priced per instructor seat,
which we expect to be our main recurring revenue. Second, one-time conversion and onboarding
services, where we digitize a program's recipe library for a fixed fee. Third, optional

curriculum alignment consulting, billed per project.
Our early pricing assumption is a license in the range of several hundred dollars per
instructor per year, with conversion packages priced by the number of recipes. These numbers
come from conversations with a small number of instructors and are not yet tested with real
purchase decisions. We expect programs to buy through department budgets or career and
technical education funds, which can mean slow sales cycles.
Competition
Instructors currently use general recipe costing tools designed for restaurants, spreadsheets
they build themselves, or the costing exercises that come with textbooks. Restaurant costing
software is powerful but is built for operators, not for teaching, and it does not generate
lesson plans or student assignments. Spreadsheets are flexible and free but time-consuming, and
they do not handle allergens or pricing updates well. Textbook exercises are easy to adopt but
use fixed prices that quickly become stale.
Our advantage is that we are built specifically for teaching: recipes become assignments,
students see live cost data, and allergens are part of the same workflow. A weakness is that
larger software companies could add an education mode to existing products, and we have not yet
shown that instructors will pay for something they can partly do with spreadsheets. Our pricing
data also depends on third-party sources, which we are still evaluating for cost and
reliability.
Team
Danielle Okafor-Reyes is a culinary arts graduate student at our university and a former line
cook and kitchen supervisor. She leads curriculum design and instructor relationships. Marcus
Tillbrook is a computer science senior who built the prototype and leads product development.
Priya Venkataraman studies business and handles customer interviews, pricing, and financial
planning. We have not yet added an advisor from the foodservice industry, though we are
speaking with two possible candidates. None of us has run a company before.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined the core concept and built a working prototype that handles recipe entry,
ingredient costing with unit conversion, food-cost percentage, and allergen flagging. We have a
basic website describing the service. Instructors at two programs, one community college and
one private school, have used the prototype with a total of roughly forty students in trial
assignments. Feedback so far has been positive about time savings, and instructors asked for
better handling of regional ingredient pricing and support for batch recipes. We have not yet
collected payment from any customer, and we have not formed a legal entity.
Our costs so far are small and have been covered personally by the team: hosting, a few
software subscriptions, and travel to visit one program. Over the next twelve months we project
spending mostly on pricing data access, part-time development help, and basic legal and
accounting setup. Our rough target is five paying programs by the end of the first year, which
would bring in revenue in the tens of thousands of dollars, not enough to cover full salaries
but enough to show demand. These projections are early estimates and will change as we learn
more.
What We Are Asking For
We are seeking prize funding to cover legal formation of the company, a one-year pricing data
subscription, and paid pilots at three to five additional programs. We would also value
mentorship from people with experience selling software to schools or colleges, introductions
to culinary program directors, and advice on how to structure pricing and contracts for public
institutions. Finally, we would welcome feedback on whether our market is large enough to
support a standalone company or whether we should position Menuschool as a feature within a
broader hospitality education offering.

Question: Share thoughts on market attractiveness and exit potential. Address whether the market would support this venture, whether the company targets the correct group, and whether the market is large enough to support scaling.
